item.title: 12 Oct 2026: Why Ganumedes Was Spirited Away
item.description:
Let’s take the seven degrees of consciousness as a series of classrooms, each having a lesson to learn: elements learn to be, animals learn to grow, humans learn to identify, heroes learn to love, daimones learn to understand, angels learn to unify, gods learn to universalize. (I am using Hierokles of Alexandria’s terminology for the beings of each degree of being, rather than my usual four-fold terminology, here.)

Let’s suppose we have a student in the human classroom, attempting to learn how to have an identity—that is, attempting to learn how to relate to the group. But humans have free will: let us suppose that the others in the classroom are peculiarly hostile to our poor student, defining them as an outsider, and shutting them out of social interaction. This is beneficial for the hostile students, of course, since such identification allows them to better develop their own identities, but it is harmful to the one student, since it prevents them from doing so. So what are they to do?

Well, perhaps the obvious option is to try to find some other group to engage with, or else develop some identity so compelling or disruptive that the others find it impossible to ignore: this would restore balance, and all the students would then continue to develop as normal.

But let us suppose that the shutting out of our student is sufficiently complete, and that the student is sufficiently discouraged and precocious, that, rather than continuing to attempt to engage with the group, they instead go on to develop their higher capacities: perhaps they try to learn compassion for the group that has so shunned them, or perhaps they try to understand the mechanics behind why things are the way they are, or so on. This is commendable, but now we have a problem! See, the student has failed to learn the lessons of their grade, and so they lack the prerequisites necessary to graduate to the next: even if they advanced, they would be unable to effectively learn the lessons there. But on the other hand, you can’t simply hold them back and make them repeat their grade: they have already moved beyond it, their interests lie elsewhere, to hold them back would be to punish them for the misbehaviors of others, for working hard, for learning; this would simply discourage them from learning in the future, which is the whole point of their existence! So the student has made a paradox for themselves: they can’t move on, but neither can they stay where they are.

What to do?

In an ideal world, perhaps the compassionate thing would be to pull the student out of school and give them a tutor who can specialize the curriculum to their peculiar needs, yes? And this is why, I think, that heroes, betrayed by Mother Earth, murder her so that they can inherit Father Sky’s kingdom. It is also why Ganumedes, with his peculiar beauty, is unfit to live with either of his brothers and is snatched up to Olumpos in a whirlwind.

So, then, the mysteries aren’t a religion for everyone. Perhaps it is correct to say, as most kinds of spirituality do, that it is best to learn to appreciate earth and live well in it; but one must recognize that this is sometimes impossible, and so it is also good, in such cases, for one “to try to escape from earth to the dwelling of the gods as quickly as one can.”

item.title: 26 Sep 2026
item.description: Reflecting back on this post from a couple years ago, a fourth, and frankly more obvious, possibility has occurred to me: Apollon is simply suggesting that, as Puthagoras was the dawn of Greek philosophy, and Plato its zenith, so too was Plotinos its twilight.

item.title: 31 Aug 2026
item.description:
Stumbled across a quote worth remembering in an otherwise uninteresting article:

When a human being becomes exhausted after making all possible sincere efforts, and cries out in despair, the highest state of devotion emerges. And during that spontaneous devotional flood, the student attains ecstasy. That is called the grace of God. In a sense this grace is unconditional, but it is still the fruit of faithful and sincere effort.

item.title: 28 Aug 2026: In Defense of White Jesus
item.description:
This came up several times in conversation in the last week, so it must be in the zeitgeist, and I figured I’d write it up.

Now, of course divinity is without form (or, indeed, without differentiation, since all is One in the spiritual world)—but here in the depths of Haides, it is very dark, and we humans often make use of crutches in order to help us connect with divinity. One of these is the construction of images depicting divinity in a symbolic sort of way, as a reminder of the gods various functions: as Sallustios says (On the Gods and the World §6), “Hints of the gods’ functions may be seen in their images.” Apollo is depicted stringing a lyre because understanding brings harmony from disparate elements. Artemis is a virgin who avoids cities for the wilderness because she is purificatory, and to become pure one must shun the multitude and seek on their own. Aphrodite is naked and has baby Eros always with her because beauty must be unconcealed in order to be appreciated, and because beauty provokes desire.

While talking with a friend about Athene, he criticized me for a depiction of Athene as specifically white, when of course gods don’t have race, and this justifies (and in fact demands) depicting Athene as black or Hispanic or some other minority race. My response to this is that doing so destroys the symbol. Perhaps you recall,

Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην, κούρην Διός, ἥ τέ τοι αἰεὶ
ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι παρίσταμαι ἠδὲ φυλάσσω,

Maid Athenaie, daughter of Zeus, who is always
standing with you and guarding you in all your endeavors!

(Homeros, Odusseia XIII 300–1.)

The point of Athene as a symbol is that she is close, she is familiar, she is always with you. To exoticize her is to miss the point, making her far away, other, alien... and how are you to use a symbol to connect with something that the symbol itself says is remote? So to a person of whatever race, it would be silly to depict Athene as anything other than similar to themselves.

In the same way, I was talking with a couple other friends who were laughing at depictions of Jesus as white, because (assuming he was a historical person rather than a mythic figure) he was of Middle-Eastern descent. But, again, Jesus as a symbol is the personal aspect of god, the mediator, your big brother—he is not supposed to be foreign or unknown, but close to you, as close as possible, and always ready to lend an ear. To depict him otherwise is, just like with Athene, to destroy the symbol.

(It always feels weird when I happen to be the one defending Christian practices! “Misery acquaints a man with strange bedfellows.”)

Since our society is actively trying to undermine these symbols, and has a motive in doing so (being materialistic or otherwise hostile to people pursuing spirituality on their own terms), I assume whatever means they use to do so amounts to intentional iconoclasm, done in bad-faith. I think we spiritual people should not defer to them, but should remember what our symbols mean and why they’re important, and push back against such means.

item.title: 26 Aug 2026
item.description: Plotinos says somewhere that the mark of a good craftsman is that he can do good work even with poor tools and materials, while a poor craftsman struggles with even the finest. It occurs to me that we have an excellent image of this in Lord Apollon, the greatest musician of all: he doesn’t play on a Stradivarius; no, he plays on a fucking tortoise-shell strung by a baby!
